AMD $AMD has two major product releases converging at the same time: Venice CPUs and the highly anticipated Helios MI400 Series.

Just three months ago, management expected server CPU revenue to grow more than 70% in 2027, while total Data Center revenue would grow “well over 100%,” driven by the Helios ramp.

Since then, AMD has raised its outlook considerably, and the two product ramps are now exceeding our original expectations.

Server CPU revenue is now expected to more than double in 2027, up from the previous outlook for 70%+ growth. Meanwhile, Data Center AI revenue (GPUs) is expected to significantly more than double.

All-in, AMD guided for companywide revenue to increase more than 80% next year, which is more than twice the company’s long-term growth model outlined at its November 2025 Analyst Day.

Perhaps the most important milestone is that AMD’s Data Center AI business is expected to surpass its server CPU business in revenue for the first time in Q4, as Helios enters a multi-gigawatt cycle with Anthropic, $META, $MSFT, OpenAI, and $ORCL deploying its new racks.

This brings us back to my July 2024 prediction that AMD’s returns would surpass Nvidia $NVDA, a call I made when Nvidia was the market darling.

Since then, AMD has gained more than 250% compared to Nvidia’s 51%, outperforming by about 5X.

And I have a hunch that gap could get wider.

en_summary: Since 2023, spot uranium price up >+50% and LT price up +60%. Utility demand core driver, not just speculation. Commodities don't rise in oversupplied market. Responds to past caution on inventories and Arrow production. Mentions $NXE.
text:
Warren, since 2023 (broadly), the spot uranium price is up > +50% and the LT price is up +60%. While some financial speculation has aided this move, utility demand has been the core driver. I know I don't have to tell you this, but commodities don't rise in price in an oversupplied market.

In Sept. 2023, you mentioned the enormous commercial inventories and the 30mil lbs/yr from Arrow that would "flood the market in a few years" as reasons for caution. The four months that followed that post, the spot price doubled and the equities tripled. And while there was again some speculators involved in that move, everyone was buying following two large RFPs that year (PG&E in Q2, KHNP in Q3) – utilities, traders, funds, and producers (Cameco, THK (KAP), UG (Orano), etc.).

I have been wrong countless times with short-term expectations, so I'm not trying to take my own victory lap regarding the commodity's trajectory. But to claim you were right about a lacking supply deficit when the information regarding the commodity's price move over the past 3 years is there for all to see – simply because the equities are getting thrashed due to AI/Vol basket correlation – is a poor take. 

I'd suggest looking at the forward curve for the commodity, including the long-term contract terms currently being signed. That's a better way to gauge where price is headed than looking at strategic commercial inventories that are not and will not be for sale, or at developers' investor presentations.

Anyh

text:
@thestreetpro

A Repeated Refrain of Mine: Buy Financials

I continue to view financials/banks as a benefit of market rotation (possibly away from technology).

* Financials, on average, are about  25% off of their 52 week highs.

* Valuations are now reasonable.

* Major money center banks and brokers have spent massive amounts on technology – a lot of which is already “sunken costs. This provides the “best in class” and largest banks (as first adopters to AI) to be differentiated against the broad universe of smaller sized banks (who will not be able to catch up and compete).

* As I see it, the yield curve will be normalizing – benefiting net interest margins and income.

* The slowdown in AI spend (which I anticipate) should elongate the domestic economic cycle – improving the credit outlook and asset growth.

* An improving equity augurs well for capital market activity.

* Finally, while the unrealized losses on their investment portfolio is underwater – the likelihood that interest rates may have peaked augurs well for that line item to appreciate in the time ahead.

Positions: Long $MS  $GS  $BAC  $C  $WFC

text:

The note is the clearest explanation so far of why Q4 came in light, how much cushion sits in the 2027 guide and how next year's build will be funded.

The ARR story:
The ARR miss is a matter of weeks. Without the Microsoft-related delays, the third-party colocation sites due in December would have taken ARR above $7bn. 

They slipped one to two months, which moves the milestone into the new year rather than removing it. This matches the shareholder letter's shift of the ~$7bn ARR target from December to February.

2027 Guidance:
Management calls the 2027 guide conservative. It is built to hold even if Nebius's own data centers are late by many months, so on-time delivery would be upside to the $12–13bn revenue outlook. 

The 800 MW–1 GW connected-power target was not repeated, and investors should assume Microsoft and other delays are factored in.

Financing:
The 2027 outlook assumes $17–20bn of customer prepayments, and a significant part of that is committed under existing contracts and paid before the capacity is delivered.

General:
Management sees third-party colocation partners as less reliable, sometimes one to two months late or more, which is why most 2027 data centers will be company-owned.

Owned sites help margins later. They put an appreciating asset on the balance sheet instead of a lease in the P&L. The full benefit appears

text:
$CBRS — the guide did the heavy lifting.

$CBRS builds wafer-scale AI chips — one giant chip instead of many small ones — and increasingly sells access to them as a cloud service rather than selling the hardware. Customers rent inference capacity, $CBRS keeps the chips and charges for use. That shift is the story: cloud revenue is growing fast while hardware sales shrink.

Today's print split in two. On the headline numbers it missed, with a wider loss. On its own core measure it beat, with core revenue of $230.9M. Then the guide did the work: next quarter is guided at $310–330M of core revenue, well above consensus, against a $26B backlog, and a new agreement with $MSFT was disclosed, size undisclosed. Shares jumped after hours.

The honest distinction: a raised guide and a big backlog prove demand is real. They do not prove profitability is near — the loss widened a lot on the headline numbers, and the gap between the core measure and the headline is wide. The reliability question from the short seller was answered by the CEO weeks ago; what this print tested was whether the economics hold up, and the cloud growth is the evidence for it.

Long term, if the cloud model scales, $CBRS becomes a recurring-revenue inference provider with a cost edge from building at wafer scale. If hardware economics or chip reliability bite, the story is the capex. The print backs the demand side. The cost side is still being proven.

$TE makes solar modules and cells in Texas. It builds the panels and sells them to developers building solar projects. Most of next year's capacity is already contracted.

Today's print missed the revenue bar by nearly 30%. The bigger item is what did not change: the financing for the Austin fab is still not closed. Talks are exclusive and it is the company's number one priority, and the build pace has been slowed to match the financing timeline. The honest distinction: contracted capacity proves customers want the product. It does not prove the factory gets built on time without the financing package. The tax-credit question is still open, not decided.

Long term, if the cells arrive on time and the financing closes, this is a US manufacturer with contracted demand in a market that needs domestic supply. If either slips, the story stretches. The print resolved neither.

text:
$NBIS — the print beat, the funding plan didn't.

$NBIS rents out AI compute. It builds data centers full of GPUs and sells the capacity to customers training and running AI models, on multi-year contracts. The model is contract-first: customers sign long deals and pay upfront, and $NBIS uses that money to build the next data center.

Today's print beat the bar on revenue. The market sold it anyway, because the funding plan is the story now. Next year's build is far bigger than next year's revenue — 2027 revenue is guided at $12–13B against $40–45B of capex — and the $7B annual recurring revenue target slipped a few months. Cash sits at $7.4B.

The honest distinction: contracted revenue proves demand is real. It does not prove the build is funded. The offset is that customers are effectively financing the expansion — prepayments plus contract-backed financing are meant to cover most of next year's build. What that does not prove is that the pace holds if a customer slows down, or if debt markets stay shut to names like this.
Long term, if it executes, the contracted backlog converts into a very large revenue base. The risk is the gap between building now and getting paid later. That gap is the whole thesis now.

zh_summary: $MPLX has now increased its quarterly distribution by 12.5% for three consecutive years! Incredible.
en_summary: $MPLX has now increased its quarterly distribution by 12.5% for three consecutive years! Incredible.
text:
$MPLX has now increased its quarterly distribution by 12.5% for three consecutive years!

Incredible distribution growth… But even more incredible considering that it’s current yield is 8.2%.

The Chowder Rule adds a stock’s dividend yield to its annual dividend growth rate to assess its combination of income and growth.

Using MPLX’s 8.2% yield and 12.5% distribution growth rate gives it a Chowder score of 20.7, comfortably above the commonly used 12-point target.

This gives them an astounding ‘Chowder Score’ of 20.7-

But understanding the business behind that income is important.

MPLX owns pipelines, storage terminals, natural-gas gathering and processing facilities, and infrastructure that separates natural gas liquids into usable products.

Customers primarily pay fees to move, store, and process energy products.

Long-term agreements with Marathon Petroleum include minimum-volume commitments and payments for reserved capacity-

Which makes cash flows FAR more predictable than those of an oil and gas producer.

Commodity prices still affect production activity and certain processing arrangements, but MPLX’s earnings are less directly dependent on the price of each barrel produced.

For businesses like this, growing distributable cash flow per unit is a primary driver of intrinsic value.

It supports the distributions investors receive, while retained cash can help fund growth and reduce debt.

Distributable cash flows per share is still well covering the distributions-
